chapters.summary: Hankerson identifies himself as chair and says the hearing will examine how Parks decides which events occur in city parks and the resulting costs and benefits. He notes cultural and recreational programming is core to the park system.
chapters.title: Chair Hankerson opens hearing on Parks Department event permitting

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Good morning, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Good morning all, my name is Ty Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I serve as the chair on the Committee of Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Today's hearing will focus on the process the Parks Department uses to determine the types of events that take place within our city's parks and what the resulting costs and benefits are to the park system.

chapters.summary: He says most events are free and run by Parks or public-private partners, while some are pay events with thousands of participants run by promoters holding permits. This creates a multifaceted approval process.
chapters.title: Hankerson describes free and ticketed park events

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The occurrence of cultural and recreational programming such as art festivals, films, and concerts have always been a core feature of the city park system.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Most of these events are free and sometimes run by parks itself or through its numerous public-private partners.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: However, some of these events are also

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: pay for events that include thousands of participants and often run by event promoters that have a permit with the parks.

chapters.summary: He details that events over 20 people require a $25 special event permit; larger or commercial events trigger concession fees, insurance, bonding, and permits from DOB or NYPD. Food or merchandise sales require a TUA permit negotiated with Parks.
chapters.title: Hankerson outlines permit tiers, fees, and ancillary permits

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: There's a multifaceted process for approving

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: these various events.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: For example, any event with more than 20 participants at minimum requires a special event permit for a non-refundable $25 fee.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As the event grows more complex, so does the process.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In the case of large events that involve more than 500 participants or may be commercial in nature,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Parks imposes additional requirements that must be fulfilled before a permit is issued.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: These can include fees based on the concession fee schedule and additional insurance or bonding obligations.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Furthermore, depending on the scope, location, and size of the event, additional permits

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: from agencies like the Department of Buildings or PD, Police Department, for potential security concerns may be necessary.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Aside from the substance of the event, other requirements can factor in too.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If food or merchandise is expected to be sold, a temporary use authorization, TUA, permit is required.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: A fee for this permit is negotiated with parks based on several factors, including the number of vendors at the event, estimated attendance, and the prices of the items being sold.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Once all the requirements have been met by the applicant, parks will issue a special event permit at their discretion.

chapters.summary: He says applicants, especially small community groups, struggle to understand requirements and denial reasons, and large events have raised concerns about parkland use, revenue, and damage. He hopes the hearing clarifies costs, benefits, and process improvements.
chapters.title: Hankerson raises concerns about permit complexity and park damage

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The complexity of this process can sometimes be problematic.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: From both the side of the event applicant and the Parks Department, as it must walk a fine line towards maintaining a vibrant parks environment that also prioritizes

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This is equitable access to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Event applicants, especially smaller community-based ones, often cite issues with not being able to fully understand what is required to secure a permit, not understanding the reasons as to why they may have been denied one.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Historically, there have been concerns raised about the amount of parkland used for large ticketed events.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The amount of revenue being generated for the event and the condition the park is left in after the event concludes.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Damage resulting from large crowds, vehicles, vendors, and bad weather during some of these events has sometimes left sections of parkland unusable for extended periods of time.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This has sometimes left many community members concerned that some large and commercial events can deprive New Yorkers of quality access to green space.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I hope this hearing results in having a better understanding of how Parks goes about approving special events, what the overall costs and benefits are to the city's open space, and whether there are ways we can improve the process to ensure the events are accessible.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: To all and are always respectful to the parks where they occur and to the communities they occur in.

chapters.summary: Hankerson notes the committee will also consider Intro 927, sponsored by Councilmembers Brooks-Powers and Shulman, to rename Shorefront Parkway between Beach 32nd Street and Beach 56th Place as Edgemere Avenue. He says it restores the historical name and reduces mail-delivery confusion.
chapters.title: Hankerson introduces Intro 927 to rename Shorefront Parkway

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'd also like to note that we will consider a bill unrelated to this topic, but an important one regardless.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro number 927, sponsored by my colleagues, Councilmember Brooks Powers and Councilmember Lynn Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Would officially rename Shorefront Parkway between Beach 32nd Street and Beach 56th Place as Edgemere Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This would result in...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: store the street to its original and historical name, and clear up a lot of confusion, specifically relating to mail delivery that has arisen over the years.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'd like to welcome the administration and the advocates that are here to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you again.

chapters.summary: Hankerson reads a statement from Councilmember Brooks-Powers explaining that USPS, Google Maps, and emergency responders do not consistently recognize Shorefront Parkway. Restoring Edgemere Avenue would improve addressing and support the future Arverne East development. Hankerson then prepares to swear in the administration.
chapters.title: Hankerson reads Brooks-Powers statement supporting Intro 927

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I do have a statement from Councilmember Brooks Powers regarding her bill.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to read it verbatim.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hankerson and members of the Committee on Parks and Recreation for hearing Intro 927 today.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro 927 is a simple bill renaming Shorefront Parkway to Edgemere Avenue between Beach 32nd and Beach 56th Place in Far Rockaway, Queens.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: We are requesting that Shorefront Parkway be renamed back to Edgemere Avenue, the name it held until a 2024 renaming, because the current street name is not consistently recognized by USPS, Google Maps, and other address systems.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This address discrepancy results in failed deliveries of mail and packages, challenges,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: for emergency responders and city service providers to locate properties quickly and accurately, and disruptions to essential services that rely on validated

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: addresses, including utility and insurance providers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Restoring the street name to Edgemere Avenue would align the address with commonly recognized mailing and mapping databases, improve public safety, and eliminate operational issues for future residents and businesses.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Notably, this stretch of street

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: runs along the future site of Arvern East, a multifaceted development that will transform 116 acres of vacant land into 1,650 new housing units, including 80% affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: We like to hear that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As well as co-op homeownership opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This change will address future challenges for the developers, future residents, and businesses at Auburn East.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Sophia Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.text: With that, we want to swear in the administration before they testify.

chapters.summary: David Cerrone identifies himself as Deputy Commissioner for Activation, Environment, and Planning at NYC Parks. He is joined by Anne McTiernan, Director of Citywide Special Event Permits and Policy, and Gabriella Capo from legislative affairs.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Cerrone introduces Parks Department panel

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ankerson, members of the Parks Committee, and other members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: My name is David Cerrone, Deputy Commissioner for Activation, Environment, and Planning for NYC Parks.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I'm joined today by Anne McTiernan, our Director of Citywide Special Event Permits and Policy, and Gabriella Capo from our Citywide Legislative Affairs team.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We are pleased to be here to testify today.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says summer 2026 was exceptionally busy with FIFA World Cup and Sail4th 250 celebrations, plus picnics, concerts, and festivals. He argues special events activate parks and bring New Yorkers outdoors.
chapters.title: Cerrone highlights busy summer and value of special events

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: As you may be aware, this past summer season was an exceptionally exciting one for NYC Parks, as our beaches, pools, parks, athletic fields, and playgrounds were as busy as they've ever been.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In addition to experiencing once-in-a-lifetime celebrations like the 2026 FIFA World Cup and Sailforth 250, or taking advantage of the free recreational summer programming offered by the agency throughout our parks,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: New Yorkers also made the most of our shared public spaces to enjoy family picnics, barbecues, and birthday parties, concerts, festivals, and other special events.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We're very proud of the role that our parks play in the city's cultural landscape.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And we believe that special events are an incredible way to bring New Yorkers out to enjoy their local park, which helps keep those spaces activated and vibrant.

chapters.summary: Cerrone explains events with more than 20 attendees need a special event permit, though permits are available for any size. He says most requests are small family events, applications are online, and the $25 fee is usually the only cost.
chapters.title: Cerrone gives overview of special event permit basics

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: For the purposes of today's oversight hearing, we'd like to offer a brief overview of our agency's special events permitting process.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We recognize that special events can provide tremendous added value to our park system, so we strive to make the permitting process as transparent and efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Our permitting staff works directly with event organizers to make their events a reality, while ensuring that proposed events are appropriate and avoid negative impacts on our beloved open spaces.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Any park event expected to have more than 20 attendees is required to have a special event permit.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Though permits are also available for groups of any size hoping to reserve a specific area in a park.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Anyone can apply for a special event permit from the agency, from organizations planning a large event for the public, to families looking to host smaller birthday parties, weddings, reunions, or barbecues.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And it is this latter category of smaller events that makes up the vast majority of permit requests submitted to the agency.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Permit applications are typically submitted through a dedicated page on our agency website.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: There is a $25 processing fee for permit applications, which allows the city to recoup some of the costs of processing applications and helps discourage attempts to monopolize permits citywide.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And for the majority of permit requests, this nominal fee is the only cost for an applicant to be able to hold their event.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says permit requests are processed in borough offices with 21 days' advance notice, but review time varies by complexity and volume. Final approvals often come closer to the event date, and amplified sound requires NYPD approval.
chapters.title: Cerrone explains borough processing and 21-day lead time

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Most special event permit requests are processed by staff.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: in our permit offices in each of the five boroughs to ensure there is ample time to properly review and discuss proposed event details with all necessary stakeholders,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: which might include other city agencies or construction contractors working on site.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We require permit requests for typical permit events to be submitted at least 21 days in advance.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: The duration of the request review for each permit from submission to approval can vary depending on the scope and complexity of the event being submitted, the volume of permit applications being processed by the permit offices.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Similarly, it is not uncommon for an event proposal to evolve and iterate as event organizers provide more information to our staff.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Which sometimes requires additional dialogue with other entities, such as the use of amplified sound for an event, which requires NYPD approval.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: As such, we ask that people apply with as much lead time as possible to ensure they can secure their desired dates.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And keep in mind that the final permit approvals and issuances are typically not issued until closer to the event date.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: However, the agency does everything in its power to expedite the review and approval of permit requests, and even though applicants are asked to submit requests at least 21 days in advance,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: This does not mean that a given request will take that long to approve.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says outright denials are less than 1% of permits and Parks almost always works with applicants on alternative dates or locations. Most permits are for small picnics, barbecues, and birthday parties.
chapters.title: Cerrone reports denials are rare and alternatives are offered

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We are pleased to report that outright den

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Niles of special event permits are exceedingly rare, making up less than 1% of the permits processed by the agency.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And in the event that proposed event location is already permitted for another event,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We are nearly always able to work with the applicant to identify alternative locations or dates for their event to carry forward.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Though the majority of our thousands of special event permits each year are issued for small picnics, barbecues, and birthday parties,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: our parks also serve as a location for larger events with a more expansive reach, such as concerts and festivals.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Though these larger events present additional considerations for the agency review, we feel that activating our parks with a wide range of recreational and cultural activity helps make them more robust and dynamic public spaces for everyone to enjoy.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says events over 500 attendees go through the citywide special events team and require a site map, production schedule, liability insurance, security bond, and site fee. They may also need FDNY, DOB, NYPD, or DOHMH permits.
chapters.title: Cerrone details large-event permit requirements

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: To ensure that larger event permit requests can

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: handled can be handled consistently and fairly any event expected to have over 500 attendees is permitted through our citywide special events team given that these events are considerably more complex than a typical small event

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: potentially disrupting access to a park or even resulting in damage to the park permit applicants for large events need to provide additional information to the agency

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: a preliminary site map and production schedule, proof of commercial general liability insurance,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: submission of a security bond to be held against damages incurred, and payment of a site fee on the concession fee schedule established by agency rules.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Additionally, depending on the proposed components of the events,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Applicants may need to secure ancillary permits from other city agencies, such as the fire department for use of a generator, department of buildings for installation of a large structure,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: the police department for safety, or the department of health and mental hygiene for food distribution.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We collaborate often with our sister agencies.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And are in constant communication with them when it comes to moving permit applications forward.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says Parks tries to accommodate applicants but cannot approve events that harm parkland or significantly interfere with other users. Denials are relatively rare and based on location, size, configuration, or natural features.
chapters.title: Cerrone explains when Parks may deny a permit

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We always try to work with applicants toward an outcome that works for everyone, but our agency is ultimately responsible for the care and protection of our city parkland for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we're not able to accommodate every aspect of each request.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: For each park.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If the requested location is inappropriate for the proposed event activity because of the park size, configuration, or natural features,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: or if the proposed activity is likely to harm the park or significantly interfere with the enjoyment of the park by other users, then the agency may have grounds to deny the permit application.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But this is relatively rare.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says Parks held nine partner forums in early 2025 with over 140 groups, redesigned the special events webpage, created a guide, and centralized policy offices. Parks is also preparing a multilingual informational handout.
chapters.title: Cerrone outlines transparency and process improvements

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Admittedly, the matrix of permits and approvals can be daunting.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: for some to navigate, especially those less familiar with the city government.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we have undertaken a dedicated effort to make our permit process more transparent and user-friendly.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In early 2025, we hosted a series of nine partner input forums in all five boroughs related to our special event permit process.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And invited representatives from park partner groups and other frequent permittees to offer feedback.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Over 140 distinct partner groups participated in these forums, providing invaluable perspective about their experience, connecting directly in person with our managers and permit coordinators,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: and sharing recommendations and knowledge with their fellow partners.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: With this feedback in mind, we redesigned our agency websites for special events permit page to display key information more clearly to applicants,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: including the creation of a special events guide with key links to other agencies for ancillary permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: To ensure greater consistency in the interpretation of agency rules and guidelines across all five boroughs, we have centralized our Special Events Permit Policy Office and our citywide Athletics Permits and Policy Office,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: working in close coordination with our borough permit offices.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We are also working on additional process improvements to come, including finalizing an informational handout that will be available in multiple languages to clearly outline things applicants should keep in mind when applying.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: for special event permits from NYC Parks.

chapters.summary: Cerrone says Parks wants robust park activity but must protect shared spaces and ensure fair access. He thanks the committee and offers to answer questions.
chapters.title: Cerrone closes with commitment to balance events and park protection

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In closing, we are committed to helping New Yorkers plan fun and creative special events in parks because we know a park with robust activity is safer and more enjoyable for everyone.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But we must still uphold our primary responsibility as the caretaker and steward of city parkland.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Our shared spaces need to be protected and used appropriately, and access must be fair.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We seek to accommodate the desired outcomes of the permit applicants while protecting the needs of everyday park users to access and enjoy the open spaces they love.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing us to testify before you today.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And for your continued advocacy and support for our city parks.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We would now be happy to answer any questions that you may have.

chapters.summary: Hankerson acknowledges Councilmember Frank Morano and Councilmember Ung on Zoom. He notes only two members are present, says he loves parks, and will ask several questions before turning to Morano.
chapters.title: Chair Hankerson acknowledges members and sets up questioning

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I do want to acknowledge that we are joined by Councilmember Frank Marano of Staten Island, the Borough of Parks.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I got that right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Councilmember Ong is also joining us via Zoom.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether it is problematic that final permit approvals are typically issued close to the event date. Cerrone acknowledges the concern, cites over 24,000 permit applications last year, and says Parks extended the application window to the Tuesday after Labor Day.
chapters.title: Hankerson challenges late permit approvals as problematic

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay, let me just state this disclaimer before I go into questioning.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I love parks, and I'm grateful for the work that you all do.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Given that it's only two of us here today, it gives me more time to ask more questions.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I do want to just ask a few questions and I'll turn it over to

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Councilor Murano, and then I'll jump back in.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Just from your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You stated in your testimony, as such, we ask that people apply with as much lead time as possible to ensure they can ensure their desired dates.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And keep in mind that final permit approvals and insurance issuances are typically not issued until closer to the event date.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Do you not see that as problematic?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We really appreciate your attention to this matter.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think as a baseline, we always want to do the best we possibly can for the public.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And that means each person that submits an application has to have a wonderful experience.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: That's our goal.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We have so many permit applications.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Last year we had over 24,000.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: This year we're actually tracking slightly ahead of that.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think we might get close to 25,000.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we've got to do our best each time.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Sometimes we're going to do better than others, honestly.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And I think as part of that, I just want to highlight some of the work that my colleague, Ann McTiernan, is doing with the citywide special events.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: When she started in this role, she sought feedback from as many different stakeholders as she could about the permit process.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And one of the things that she heard and that we heard as an agency is that applicants felt like they needed more time to apply for a permit.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And there wasn't enough time to apply for events that they wanted to plan.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So for an example, here we are in 2026.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: A few years ago, if you wanted to apply for a permit in 2027, you couldn't do that until the second week of November.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: What Ann did is she worked with our council's team and made a rule change so that now people can apply the Tuesday after Labor Day.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So really by about a little bit more than two months, extending the time that permit applications can be submitted to the agency.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we do hear you.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think our goal is to be able to get back to everybody as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And in some cases, we're going to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In other cases, it's going to be a little bit tougher.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think in the case of being able to allow the public to submit permit applications earlier, in theory, if someone were to submit

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: for an application in 2027 and they submitted on that Tuesday after Labor Day, they would be applying for a permit application up to 14 months in advance.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So in instances like that, that's on the extreme end, of course.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But the permit staff in each borough is going to focus on what's coming up sooner.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So they're still going to be focused on September, October, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And then also, depending on the time of year, in the month.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: of June and July, just those few weeks, we're roughly going to process probably close to 20% of our permits, maybe in like, you know, eight or so percent of the time.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So, you know, and it's going to depend how quickly we're able to respond.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But our goal is to be as responsive as possible to everyone who submits an application.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks how a small community group with limited resources can plan when it may be denied days before its event. Cerrone cites denial rates from 2022-2025, all under 1%, and says Parks' directive is to find a pathway to yes.
chapters.title: Hankerson presses on late denials for small community groups

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I mean, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But if it's typical for you all to not approve or deny until closer to the date, let's...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Just say if I'm a community-based organization, a small group, and we have limited resources and we've worked hard to plan this event that's supposed to happen within our local park,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: and then it's not until a few days before that we hear, hey, you can't have your event, it's been denied.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Does the Parks Department not see that as problematic?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So I think in instances like that, when we think about denials, denials have been historically, we've looked back over the past several years, it's been less than 1% of the permits that we've processed.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we're in the range, actually.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: My eyes are not as good as they were, I'm realizing today.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: No worries.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In 2022, we processed 23,948 permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: 47 were denied.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In 2023, we processed 23,844 permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: 18 were denied.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In 2024, we processed 23,507 permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: 37 were denied.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And in 2025, we processed 24,241 permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And 23 were denied.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So it's a small percentage.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I want you to know that when we approach a permitting,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Our goal and the directive from our commissioner is to find a pathway to yes.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we work as hard as we possibly can to find alternatives so that we don't have to deny.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But it's true, Council Member, there will be instances exactly like the one you described.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And we want to keep working to make sure that we're doing better and doing as well as we can.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And to that end, you know, one thing that we're proud of, and I know the commissioner is proud of, is that if you were to look us up on the website and you wanted to find your borough office, right away you would find a phone number.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You would find a person to call.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And you could get on the phone and you could speak to a special event coordinator and ask them about your permit.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And they would tell you what the latest was and try to work with you to a solution.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But also, if you know, if there's an organization that you're working with that has called you, please tell Ann and I, and we want to work with them because we deeply care about them having the best experience.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And we want to make things work for them as well.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether Parks can provide denial data by borough. Cerrone says yes and gives an example of denying a polo match with horses on the Great Lawn because it was inappropriate for the landscape.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks for denial data by borough

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Given the less than 1% of denials, does the data demonstrate the locations of those denials by borough?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So, yeah, that can be one of the instances in which it come up.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You hit it exactly.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If someone applies for an event in a park, and I think this would be like a bigger event, so I'm not talking about a picnic or like, you know, a family gathering or even a wedding.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But if they wanted to do something that was larger and, you know, it just was too big for the park or it was inappropriate for the landscape.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You know, the example that comes to mind is I think a year or two ago, we got a request to do a polo match with horses on the Great Lawn.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And we couldn't approve that.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We had to deny that because it was just, it was not appropriate for the landscape.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: To have the horses there.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Can parks provide the data based on location of denials?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Awesome.

chapters.summary: Hankerson confirms staffing counts: Staten Island 3, Queens 6, Manhattan 8, Brooklyn 5, Bronx 8. Cerrone says Brooklyn may be lower due to retirements and a staffing transition, and will follow up with precise numbers.
chapters.title: Hankerson questions borough permit staffing levels

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I want to just acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilman Berlinda Lee.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I do want to, before I go to Councilman Murano,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You mentioned that folks can pick up the phone and call the permit office and speak to a permit representative.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I do want to talk about the permit offices just really briefly.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Folks are assigned to each permit office by borough.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Bear with me just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In Staten Island, there are three coordinators.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In Queens, there are six.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In Manhattan, there are eight.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: In Brooklyn, there are five.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And in the Bronx, there are eight.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Eight?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I have this correct.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Staten Island, there are three.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Queens, there are six.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Manhattan, there are eight.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Brooklyn, there are five.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The Bronx, there are eight.

utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: That's by borough, yes.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Out of curiosity, why does Brooklyn only have five?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So I would have to get back to you on the precise amounts.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You know, there are fluctuations in staffing.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I can tell you in Brooklyn, they had a longstanding director, Nancy Melissas, who was a wonderful, wonderful colleague and so knowledgeable about Brooklyn Parks.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And she had spent decades working in Brooklyn doing the permitting system, and she recently retired.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And then one of her colleagues moved on to become the director of the permit office in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So they may be a little bit lower because of that staffing transition, but we're happy to follow up with your office and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: more precise answers.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether permit-office staff receive cultural training. Cerrone says all new Parks employees get two days of orientation including sensitivity and cultural training, and the citywide special events team will retrain after parade and marathon season.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about cultural and sensitivity training

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Given the permit offices tend to be the front-facing division or unit within the Parks Department engaging with community members, various cultures, are they required to take any type of cultural training?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So every employee that starts with parks goes through an orientation for two days.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And part of that orientation involves sensitivity training and cultural training and wanting to make sure that we're always interacting with the public in the most positive way possible.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And I can tell you, Councilmember, that is a top priority for the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I can also say that with regard to our citywide special events training, as soon as this, after the parade and the marathon, there's a little bit of a better time to do retraining.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And we're going to be retraining with our staff in the citywide event.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So it's not just when we start, but it's making sure that we're updating those trainings and refreshing them and doing that time and time again.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Our goal is to be the best that we can possibly be as public servants.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And that means when the public or when a council member interacts with us, that they feel good about that experience.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are the trainings...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Led by outside organizations or are they conducted in-house?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: They're conducted in-house.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We have a dedicated team that is the Parks Training Academy that does trainings on customer service and several other areas where we want to make sure that our staff is able to constantly get that kind of update.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And I can say they're very accomplished, and they take their job very seriously, and they continue to look at best practices for teaching agency personnel and updating them on how standards evolve.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks if the committee can sit in on a training. Cerrone is open, and Gabriella Capo says she will check with the Parks Academy and follow up.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks whether committee can observe Parks Academy training

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You know, I can promise you that this committee is much larger than the two of us.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Would the agency be willing for the committee to sit through one of the trainings?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I believe so, but Gabriella, I'm going to turn it to you.

utterances.speaker: Gabriella Capo
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Gabriella Capo
utterances.text: That's something I'd have to check with the Parks Academy.

utterances.speaker: Gabriella Capo
utterances.text: I'm not sure what our track record is of doing it in the past, but I'm happy to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks Anne McTiernan what Parks asks elected officials hosting back-to-school giveaways. McTiernan says Parks asks about site layout, production schedule, staffing, and queueing, and also asks the value of book bags to understand the giveaway.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about book-bag value questions at giveaways

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned Anna represents Citywide.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Anna, how are you?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I do have a question for you, and then I'm going to turn it over to my colleague for some questions, and I'll jump back in.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Elected officials tend to host several events within parks across the city.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: One of the events that we tend to host, particularly around August, September, are back-to-school giveaways.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Partnering with local non-for-profits, CBOs,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: and sometimes some private partners as well to give book bags to the community.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Typically, when you all are reviewing such a permit, what are the questions that are asked of the elected officials office or whomever may be hosting this back to school giveaway?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In the park?

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilperson.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: We ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: about their site layout, their production schedule, when vendors are going to be arriving,

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: if there's any run of show, any speaking portion, when they're setting up the location for the giveaway, making sure that they're sufficiently staffed and there's a queue line set up so that there's

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: an orderly way to receive the backpacks by the public.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: So questions like that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Is it common practice for the department to ask the applicant the value of the book bags?

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: That is a question that we do ask.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What's the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: Just understand the price point of the item that's going to be given away.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: But really, a lot of times with giveaways, the value is not as important as making sure you have enough for the public that's going to be coming to the giveaway so that there's not a point.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: During the event where we've run out and you have a long line of people waiting, we want to make sure that folks are receiving the giveaway and able to

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: partake in the actual excitement of the event.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: So those sort of questions are asked.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: A lot of times asked by our security partners at NYPD as well and the mayor's office.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: These are common questions.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: NYPD and the mayor's office tend to also ask about value of items being distributed.

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: And then to make sure you have a quantity that is sufficient for the expected attendance of your event.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Excuse my short memory.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What was the reason for asking the value of the book bags?

chapters.summary: Cerrone says each event has different components and some judgment calls are made. He acknowledges questions can make applicants feel negative and says the agency wants to learn and do better.
chapters.title: Cerrone addresses customer-service concerns in permit questioning

utterances.speaker: Anne McTiernan
utterances.text: To just make sure that there's an understanding of the value of the item that's being given away.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Councilmember, if I may, I think, you know, in certain instances, you know, when a, you know, every event has different components.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: There's, you know, there will be some judgment calls, notwithstanding anything that my colleague said.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But I think the key sentiment here is, like, if we're, whether it's an elected official or a member of the public,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Our goal is we want that person to have a positive takeaway from their experience.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And if they're asked a question that makes them feel less than positive, we want to understand that and we want to do better next time.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And, you know, I think.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: A lot of our special event associates are early on in their career.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: They're learning this complicated work.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: There is a lot to know here because each event is a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And I can assure you that if a question like that comes up, it's not coming from a bad place, but it doesn't mean that it's necessarily the right place.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: question in that moment and in that situation.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So in any instances, whether it's an elected official or whether it's a member of the public, we want to do our best every single day to make sure that the way that they're experiencing that interaction with the public servant

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: is positive.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And, you know, I suspect, you know, if we were to talk about it, there are probably other questions we could have asked to, you know, to get the same amount of information and to have that person feel better about it.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So just know that everything we do is trying to come from the best place, but we also want to learn from things that we haven't done correctly in the past and be better in the future.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether the process for questioning applicants is reviewed through Parks Academy sensitivity training. Cerrone says he will get back to the committee on the exact training layout and scenarios.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks if permit questioning is covered in sensitivity training

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And I personally am dedicated to working with you, any of your colleagues, and Anna's as well, or any other stakeholders, event applicants, so that we're able to help them proceed with their event

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: in the best way possible, but also in a way that people feel positive about.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I just want to kind of moonwalk back a little bit to the Parks Academy training.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: When we're talking about questions that are posed to applicants that are applying for permits,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: is that process, does that process go through the Parks Academy sensitivity training as well?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Is that reviewed by any staff members or is it just something that's...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Made up within that team or division or unit of people?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: That's a good question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on the exact layout of the training and the different areas and scenarios that are covered during the training.

chapters.summary: Hankerson acknowledges Councilmember Chris Marte and says he does not want to use all the time. He turns questioning over to Councilmember Frank Morano.
chapters.title: Hankerson acknowledges Marte and turns to Morano

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Chris Marte.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Morano notes fewer than 1% of applications are denied and asks who represents the park user who never applied. Cerrone says Parks relies on public feedback, borough offices, 311, and prioritizes youth permits for athletic fields.
chapters.title: Morano asks who advocates for non-applicants in permit process

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I don't want to take up all the time, so I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Murano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to start with something that I wouldn't have thought to ask you about, but for your testimony, something that I actually think is good news.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You said that fewer than 1% of special event permit applications are denied, and I'm certainly glad to hear Parks is generally willing to work with people rather than looking for reasons to tell them no.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because obviously if you're a civic association or a veterans group, a youth group, whoever, or just a family trying to have an event in your neighborhood park, the last thing you need is another city bureaucracy making your life more difficult.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But the one question that I guess I never thought of is that statistic.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: raises somewhat of a different question for me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If the system is designed to get almost every applicant to yes, who in the process is representing the person who never submitted an application?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The applicant has somebody advocating for their event, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Who's advocating for the kid that shows up Saturday morning wanting to use the field or the senior who is walking the same path every morning?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Who's advocating for the family that shows up at the park and discovered that the place that they normally use isn't available?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Where does that person exist, if anywhere, in the permitting process?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So that's an excellent question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And, you know, it's something that we think about.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We really do rely on the public to tell us if there is, you know, if there's concerns about an event.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You know, generally that does happen.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: It tends to be with bigger events.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You know, kind of the example of the kid who wants to use a field.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Most of, you know, admittedly it is separate from this office.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Anne and her colleagues do the special events.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Our other colleague, you know, Ken Conyers, does athletic fields and permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But I know in that system they do prioritize youth permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So in instances like that, if it's a field, chances are it's being used by a youth group.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And so they would, you know, for like baseball, it's harder to do kind of like a pickup game.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean that someone wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: be there with a friend or parent just to kind of hit the ball around or play catch.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we do want to strike a balance.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Certainly, you know, we also, you know, are in close contact with the borough permit offices who are, you know, they're not separate from the rest of the borough team.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So they're there with the borough commissioner.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: They're there with, you know, the park managers.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And they're always talking about what they're seeing in their parks.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So, you know, it could come up through there.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: It could also come up through the public calling us, either calling the borough office, either through 311, calling the special events office.

chapters.summary: Morano says losing field access is especially harmful in the outer boroughs and asks if Parks measures displacement. Cerrone says it is hard to measure, but Parks checks for programming conflicts before permitting and will work with specific constituents.
chapters.title: Morano asks how Parks measures displacement of regular users

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But generally, if there's feedback about like, hey, this is a little bit too much.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: It would be around some of the larger events.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think it's particularly important in the outer boroughs and places like Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you lose access to a particular field or park space, there isn't necessarily another comparable facility three blocks away.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So does parks actually measure displacement beyond the anecdotal example that you cited?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you know how often permitted events cause regular park programming or ordinary recreational activity used to be moved or canceled?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: It's another, I think, really good question that is, you know, I can't tell you that I've, like, I've had that question posed to me before.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think offhand it would be a hard thing to measure, but one thing we do before we permit is we look for conflicts, and that is something

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: that can add a little bit, Chair, to the process.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we will look to see, is there other programming here?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Is there another permitted event here?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Is the agency doing something so that we're not inadvertently kind of making a mistake and, hey, we're going to program your event, but we're also, our colleagues in public programs, we're doing a shape-up program.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So we can avoid those things.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think it's harder to look at displacement without knowing who the user was that had wanted to use that space.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But if there's a specific park, a specific field or other amenity that you're hearing about that maybe we haven't heard about, like we will work with your office, we will work with your team,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: we will be in touch with that individual if you want to share their information to figure out what's happening and to try and find the right balance for that.

chapters.summary: Morano asks Parks to track total park days lost to setup, event, breakdown, and restoration. Cerrone says Parks tracks event dates but not full displacement, notes that only portions of parks are usually closed, and says 75% of permits are for 100 people or fewer.
chapters.title: Morano asks how many park days are lost to events

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In that vein, the...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Committee's briefing says that parks considers not just the event itself, but preparation and cleanup time when determining the impact on ordinary park users.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So here's a number that I would really like to know, and I think you probably do have access to.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many park days?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do New Yorkers lose every year to special events?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And by park days, I mean the entire period when the public can't fully use that space, the setup, the event itself, breakdown, and restoration.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you track that?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if not, I think we should.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Yeah, that's another good question.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We track the events, so we know when the event starts and when the event ends.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If it's a smaller event, there's probably not going to be much set up for a birthday party or things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If it's a larger event that involves bringing infrastructure into the park, then we will track it.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I think where it might get a little bit tricky, but, Councilmember, not that we couldn't start to kind of figure something out, is...

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Oftentimes, it's not the entire park that is being taken off offline.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: It's just a portion of the park.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But I also just want to mention, you know, in the testimony, apologies, I didn't really get into the specifics, but

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: just for reference, and we have found that this tends to hold true over the years, 75% of the permits that we process are going to be for 100 people or less.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: 95% of them are going to be for 500 people or less.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And even though 500 people, it's not like a tiny amount of people or a little bit less than that, you know, those are events that we have generally found are going to be less impactful on the experience of other park users.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But not to say that that can't happen.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And also to your very good point, not to say that that couldn't happen with an athletic field or those permits.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But I just want to stress we are ready and...

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: and willing to work with you, your team, and any constituents if they have concerns about being displaced.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Because as much as humanly possible, we want a system that works for everybody.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks what interagency collaboration looks like for permits. Cerrone says larger events involve site visits with NYPD, FDNY, DOHMH, DOB, and CECM, plus meetings on security, transportation, and promotion.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks how Parks collaborates with other agencies

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thanks, sir.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Before I go to Councilmember Lee, I do want to just kind of...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Jump on that bandwagon really quickly and ask a couple of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You mentioned that Parks Department has to collaborate with other city agencies oftentimes for permits.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What does that collaborative process look like between the agencies?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: What it looks like could change from time to time.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Generally, it's for the events that are going to be larger in scale, that will be over 500 people.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And what it looks like is a site visit with other agencies that are impacted.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Many times it's the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If there are generators or things like that being used for them, it could be FDNY.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If there's food, it could be DOHMH.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If there is a stage or a tent of a large size, I want to say 10 to 12 feet, but I don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: It could be the Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If it's more involved than that, it will involve interagency meetings with CECM, the mayor's office for CECM.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: citywide event coordination and management.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And that could be kind of like a series of meetings where we have one meeting that will focus on security, another meeting that will focus on transportation, how are we getting everybody there?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And of course, the MTA and DOT would be part of that.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Another meeting that would talk about how they're advertising and promoting the event.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And then there'll be subparts to that for

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether food, amplified sound, vending, and merchandise permits can be handled through one application. Cerrone says no, applicants must go to each agency separately, though mobile vendors may already have DOHMH permits.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks if one application can cover multiple permits

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: an event that is a large-scale event, we have to share the talent and the performers with NYPD so that they can also review and make sure that they are comfortable with it.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: So it varies.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Just from my own understanding, and I'm going to turn it over to Councilor Burley,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If I'm applying for an event, for an event application, I'm applying and I am serving food,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I may have amplified sound, is that going to require me to apply for a permit from the Parks Department?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: A sound permit from the police department, a vendor permit from Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, and let's say I'm selling merchandise, a t-shirt or something,

utterances.text: a TUA from Parks.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Is that going to require all four permit applications?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Or is there

utterances.text: a centralized location where I just put in one application and it kind of just checks off the boxes?

utterances.text: It's the former, unfortunately, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We haven't reached that level of sophistication.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: You know, I would say perhaps the only caveat that if

chapters.summary: Hankerson says CBOs get frustrated by fragmented applications and asks whether Parks has considered working with OTI to centralize them. Cerrone says that conversation has not been initiated but Parks is open to presentations and simplifying some permits.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about centralizing permits through OTI

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: If you are working with the food element, if you are working with, let's just say, like a mobile vendor, they may already have their DOHMH permitting in place.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: They probably do.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And in which case, then it would just be a matter of sharing that documentation with parks as part of the TUA process.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Has the agency considered working with, I want to say it's Do It.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: OTI?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: To potentially, or to explore ways to maybe centralize everything.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: No, no, no, it works.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I've received a number of calls, and since being in this particular role, calls from across the city now from CBOs who

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: tend to have a difficult time applying for a permit, especially given that they have to go to these different places and locations, and they get frustrated, and then ultimately they just throw up their hands and say, forget it.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And then the community loses out on what I think would be valuable services and or community events because the process seems like it's working against them and not necessarily working for them.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So is that a conversation that has been had or could potentially be had to see if we can kind of centralize this permit process, application process?

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: I don't believe that's a conversation that we've initiated with them yet.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We have focused on a lot of other process improvements.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And I just want to say, first and foremost, if there are CBOs,

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: council member in your district or in a district of one of your colleagues, we're happy to either in person to give a presentation on the process and have our borough colleagues join us as well.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We're also happy to do that remotely depending on someone's schedule.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We can do that during the day.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: We can do that later in the day.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: To help walk them through that process.

chapters.summary: Hankerson acknowledges Councilmembers Salaam, Sanchez, and others joining. He turns questioning over to Councilmember Linda Lee.
chapters.title: Hankerson acknowledges more members and turns to Lee

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: And we're continuing to make enhancements to the application system itself, similar to some recent enhancements that have been made under the ball field and athletic permits

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: side of the application process so that people have a better sense of when they submit an application, if that location is already reserved.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: With another special event permit.

utterances.speaker: David Cerrone
utterances.text: But yeah, we can certainly look into what the process would be to try and simplify things for like an amplified sound permit or maybe a permit from the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I want to just mention that we've been joined by council members.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Salam online and now Councilmember Pierina Sanchez in person.

chapters.summary: Lee seconds the request to join applications and asks again how many events permitting staff are in Queens and on the citywide team. Cerrone says Queens has six and citywide has eight.
